event: Elsie wakes before dawn in the attic. It is the nineteenth, the day before Midsummer.
She lies still and listens to the bakery waking under the boards. Her stomach is fluttery.
She thinks of tomorrow: the dark water, the boats, Cora saying thieves carry knives.
She sits up by the round window and takes the second glove off the sill beside the first.
She knits the second finger by the grey light, measuring it against the first glove's.
She tells Moonpenny it's Midsummer Eve, and that she has a fluttery feeling and can't think why.
She decides the fluttery feeling wants baking. It always does.
Downstairs Mrs Merriweather is sliding loaves out. Elsie asks if she may use the oven tonight.
Mrs Merriweather says after the shop shuts, when the oven's cooling, and mind the peel.
Elsie pays her five pips: three for a crock of honey, one for butter, one for a bag of flour.

changes.note: Elsie pays Mrs Merriweather for honey, butter and flour: 5 pips, 208 → 203

event: She asks for the honey to be left out on the counter tonight. Mrs Merriweather grunts that it will.
Elsie looks at the empty blue plate in the window. She smiles at it on her way out.
At seven Cora is on the guild hall steps, ledger under her arm. Elsie runs up them two at a time.
Elsie says good morning, it's Midsummer Eve. Cora says, Fairweather. Her eyes go to Elsie's hair.
Cora says, low, that her clip is crooked. She straightens it with two long fingers and steps back.

event: Inside, Noor is at her corner table in her ring of empty ones, in the green coat, with her coffee.

memory.fact: Folk in the guild hall keep clear of the corner table where Noor sits alone.

event: Elsie buys a second cup of coffee at the counter, black, strong, nothing in it, for two pips.

changes.note: Elsie buys Noor a second black coffee at the guild counter: 2 pips, 203 → 201

event: She carries it across the boards and sets it by Noor's first cup. She knocks twice and sits.
Noor looks at the two cups. She says she hasn't finished the first. Elsie says that one's for later.
Elsie says, Noor, it's tomorrow. She asks again: will she come out on the Mere with them?
Noor says, flat, that boats sink round her. She said so yesterday, and she meant it.
Elsie says Tilly's floating vials haven't changed either, and Tamsin can still swim.
Noor says things go wrong near her in the dark, worse than cups. Lines snap. Lanterns go out.
Elsie says Cora has a lantern that drove a barrow-wight back, so a little dark won't mind it.
Noor looks over at Cora by the clerk's desk. Cora looks back, level, over her ledger. Neither nods.
Noor says the others won't want her in their boat. Elsie says she drew Noor in already, with them.
She opens her notebook to the Midsummer page and shows Noor the boat with the five heads.
She points to the head with the long straight hair. She says, that one's you.
Noor looks at the little drawn head a long time. Her gloved finger comes up and almost touches it.
She says the hair's wrong. It's longer than that. Elsie fixes it there and then.
Noor turns her cup a quarter turn. She says: I'll sit at the back. Not near the lantern.
Elsie says yes, the back, wherever she likes. She doesn't squeal. Both hands go over her mouth.
Noor's ears go pink under her hair. She says, dryly, that she can still hear Elsie not squealing.
Elsie takes Noor's gloved hand across the table and squeezes it hard, both her hands round it.
Noor lets her. Her fingers in the black leather close round Elsie's, a little, and hold.
Tilly bursts in with Ines in tow, talking, a corked vial on a string swinging from each hand.
Tilly says she was up half the night at Ines's and she has made the floating vials, look, six.
Tilly says they bob, they've been tested in Ines's washtub, and only one went off a little.
Ines whispers that it was only a small bang. Her black lace has a singed spot on its sleeve.
Ines sits down beside Noor again, close, her lace touching Noor's coat. Noor's cup stays put.
Noor frowns at her cup. Elsie sees her frown at it, and sees her give up frowning, a little.
Elsie says Noor's coming tomorrow. Tilly shrieks and drops a vial. It bounces and doesn't break.
Tilly picks it up and puts it into Noor's gloved hand. She says that one's yours, it's lucky.
Noor holds the vial up to the light and turns it. She doesn't say thank you. She pockets it.
Elsie takes the folded barge notice to the clerk's desk. She asks to add a fourth name.
Noor has followed her. She tells the clerk her own name: Noor Haddad. The clerk's pen hangs.
The clerk looks up at Cora. Cora says, without looking up, that it's in order. She writes it in.
Noor watches her name go into the guild book under three others.
She says, very dry, that four is a lot of people to sink. Her voice doesn't come out very dry.
Tamsin swings in through the doors from the docks with Margery on her back, grinning.
She hears it from Tilly in three words and whoops. She claps Noor on the shoulder, hard.
Tamsin's bootlace snaps. She looks at it, then at Noor, and laughs till she leans on the desk.
Tamsin says four in a boat is better than three, and the boat had better be a big one.
Ines whispers to Elsie that she'll watch the fireworks from the shore tomorrow, with Biscuit.
She says she'll look for their boat. She goes home to sleep, small and black in the bright doorway.
Tamsin says the festival lends the boats from the Lantern Steps. They should go and see theirs.
At nine on the Lantern Steps a brisk grey woman with a slate is counting rowing boats.
She is Odile Marsh, the festival master. She reads the stamp on Elsie's notice and grunts.
Odile looks at Cora's coat, then at Elsie. She says, so you're the Enthraller's lot. Can you row?
Tamsin says she grew up on a barge. Odile says a barge isn't a boat, but it'll do.
Odile points out their boat: small, green-painted, number eleven, tied low at the bottom step.
She shows them the hooded lantern on its pole at the bow, and the brass bell under the seat.
She says ring the bell the moment they see a black punt with muffled oars. Ring first, think after.
She says the thieves cut lantern boats loose in the dark and strip them out on the water.
She says most run from a bell. Some don't. She looks at Margery when she says it.
Odile says they may take eleven out in the shallows this morning to learn her. Bring her back dry.
Noor stays on the top step. She says she'll get in a boat tomorrow, not before. Once is plenty.
Tamsin hops down into the boat. It barely rocks under her. She holds up a hand for Elsie.
Elsie steps in. The boat tips and she sits down hard on the middle seat, laughing.
Tamsin sits behind her on the same seat. She says Elsie's going to row, and Tamsin will teach her.
Tamsin reaches round Elsie from behind and puts Elsie's hands on the oars, then her own over them.
Tamsin's chest is warm against Elsie's back through the cream halter. Her chin is by Elsie's ear.
Tamsin says, gruff, in her ear: dip, pull, lift, back. Elsie's hair tickles her nose.
They pull out from the steps together. Elsie feels Tamsin's arms working round her, hard and sure.
Elsie says it's like dancing. Tamsin goes quiet. Her ears, by Elsie's cheek, go red.
Elsie leans back into her to see her face. Tamsin says, roughly, to look where they're going.
Tamsin takes her hands away to let Elsie try alone. Elsie's left oar skims the water and catches.
The oar jerks back. Elsie tips straight back off the seat into Tamsin's lap, legs in the air.
She lies there looking up at Tamsin upside down and laughs until she can't breathe.
Tamsin stares down at her. She doesn't laugh at first. Her hands hover over Elsie, not touching.
Then Tamsin laughs too, and lifts her back up onto the seat by the waist, as if she weighs nothing.
On the steps Cora has stopped writing. Elsie waves an oar at her. Cora looks down at her ledger.
Elsie rows them in alone, crooked. Tamsin says she's a natural, a natural disaster.
Tilly tests a floating vial off the bottom step. It bobs. She claps. Noor watches it bob.
Tilly says the bobbers will hold one person up each, if the person holds on and doesn't panic.
Noor says, from the top step, that she'll panic. Tilly says then she'll hold on very hard.
Elsie climbs out and sits on the step below Noor. She leans back against Noor's knees unasked.
Noor goes stiff. After a while one gloved hand comes down and rests on the top of Elsie's head.
Elsie shuts her eyes in the sun. Noor's hand stays there, light, the leather warm from the sun.
Elsie takes out the second glove and knits the second finger on the step, against Noor's knees.
Cora's ledger lies open on her knee beside them. The page reads: Lantern Steps. Skills used, none.
At noon Tamsin buys five hand pies from a stall at the top of the steps, a pip each.
Noor reaches into her coat to pay. Tamsin says she feeds the party, and Noor's on the notice now.
Noor takes the pie. She holds it a moment in both gloved hands. She eats it all.
Cora takes hers from Tamsin with a small inclined head. She eats standing up, looking at the water.
Tamsin counts on her fingers between bites. Twelve lanterns for tomorrow. Eight short for the house.
She stops. She looks at Noor. Four on the notice now. Twelve doesn't go eight and four.
Elsie says Noor gets a whole share, of course she does. She says it at once, not even thinking.
Tamsin says course she does, and goes on frowning at her fingers, trying to make it go.
Noor says flatly that she wants no share. She's coming to see fireworks from a boat that sinks.
Elsie says she gets a share and they'll argue about it after. Noor says: ask me tomorrow.
Tamsin snorts pie crumbs. Tilly laughs so hard she has to lie down on the warm step.
Tilly says she has to go and brew more bobbers before the light goes. She runs off up the steps.
Noor gets up. She says she'll be here at dusk tomorrow, at the back, and goes off along the Mere.
Elsie watches her go. Noor doesn't look back. At the corner she does, once, quickly.
Tamsin says she wants to go to Coin Street. She wants to ask the agent if he'll wait two days.
At one the letting agent on Coin Street mops his forehead behind a desk heaped with keys.
Tamsin asks if he'll hold the blue-door house till the twenty-first. They'll have the gold by then.
He says he can't hold it, he's sorry, my dear. It's still whoever brings four suns first.
Elsie asks him straight out when the others will bring theirs. He looks at her a moment.
He says the C-rank party say after Midsummer. The other party that looked say the twenty-second.
Tamsin counts. The barge pays on the twenty-first, the morning after. That's a day ahead of both.
She says, if they're paid on time. If the barge job goes right. If they keep the boat upright.
The agent says, not unkindly, that he'll be in his office at eight on the twenty-first.
Elsie thanks him. She promises him a honey cake on the twenty-first, warm, and means it.
Out on Coin Street Tamsin presses her knuckles to her mouth. She says a day ahead is ahead.
Elsie hugs her round the middle, axe and all. Tamsin hugs back hard enough to lift her off her feet.
Tamsin says she's off to the docks, to leave a letter for Mum at the wharf office about the house.
Elsie says she has shopping on Spindle Lane. She looks at Cora. She says it's a secret shopping.
At half past two on Spindle Lane Elsie goes into the wool shop with the grey skeins in its window.
Cora comes in after her, as she must. She stands just inside the door with her ledger.
Elsie says the second glove will run out of wool before the last finger. She needs one more skein.
She takes down three grey skeins. They are nearly the same grey and not quite.
She turns round and holds the first skein up beside Cora's face. Cora goes still.
Elsie goes up on her toes to see better. She holds the second skein up, close, by Cora's cheek.
She looks into Cora's eyes from a hand's breadth away, very seriously, and then at the wool.
Cora doesn't move. She doesn't breathe, Elsie thinks. Colour comes up along her cheekbones.
Elsie holds up the third skein. She says, that one, beaming. That's exactly the right grey.
Cora says, not quite steadily, that she had better not ask what it's the right grey of.
Elsie says she'd better not, because Elsie can't lie, and then the surprise would be spoiled.
Elsie pays four pips for the skein. She tucks it into her satchel with the needles.
Outside a flower seller has lavender. Elsie buys one sprig for a pip and smells it.
Cora asks, very evenly, who the lavender is for. Elsie says it's for someone she loves.
Cora says nothing at all. She looks at the lavender in Elsie's hand for a long moment.
Elsie tucks the sprig into her satchel beside the wool and buckles it shut. She hums.
They walk back toward the guild hall. Elsie knits the second finger as she goes, down to the tip.
She shapes it off and holds the glove up to the sun. Thumb and two fingers. Two more to go.
Cora watches the glove go back into the satchel. She shifts her ledger to her other arm.
At six the porters drag the tall doors shut. Cora stops on the top step, where she goes off duty.
She says, Fairweather, and inclines her head. Then she says the Mere is cold at night, even now.
She says to wear something warm tomorrow. Over the halter. Something with sleeves.
Elsie says she has a shawl somewhere. She says, or Cora could lend her the coat again, like before.
Cora's mouth opens. It shuts. The tips of her ears go pink above her collar.
Elsie looks up at her. She asks, quietly, why Cora said that isn't why, yesterday, by the threads.
Cora looks past her at the square. She says, not tonight.
Elsie asks, tomorrow? Cora is quiet a long time. She says, perhaps.
Elsie laughs. She says everyone's saying tomorrow today. Noor, and Cora, and tomorrow's Midsummer.
Cora's mouth goes in at one corner. It is almost a smile. She goes down the steps toward Wick Lane.
At the second bridge she looks back. Elsie is still on the step. She waves with both arms.
At seven the shop is shut and the oven cooling. Elsie ties on an apron and gets out the flour.
She makes honey cakes for the boat. Enough for five, and some over, and some over again.
Mrs Merriweather puts the crock of honey on the counter and goes up to bed without a word.
Elsie hums as she beats the butter. She doesn't know she's humming.
Someone taps on the shop window. Amara stands outside under the red lantern, hands behind her back.
Elsie lets her in, floury to the elbows. Amara's just in time: Elsie can't beat and pour at once.
Amara has never been inside the Honeycomb. She looks round at the trays and shelves.
Amara says she couldn't sleep, and she thought the window would be lit. It is.
Elsie gives her an apron and a wooden spoon. Amara holds the spoon as if it might bite.
Elsie stands behind her at the bowl, her hand over Amara's on the spoon, to show her the stir.
Amara goes very still under her hand. Elsie stirs with her, round and round. Amara breathes out.
Elsie lets go. Amara keeps stirring by herself. She doesn't look round. Her neck has gone warm.
They spoon the batter into the tins side by side. Their elbows bump. Amara laughs, startled.
Amara says, to the batter, that her mother has had a gown made for her. Gold, for the barge.
She tried it on today. She stood in it before the long glass and couldn't make a sound.
Elsie asks if she's told her mother yet. Amara shakes her head. She says, have you told yours?
Elsie says she tells her mother everything, every week. She doesn't know how not to.
Amara asks what Elsie would do, if she were her. She asks it to the tins.
Elsie thinks. She can't lie. She says she'd tell her mother, because her mother would want to know.
Amara says, quietly, that Elsie doesn't know her mother. Elsie says no. But she knows Amara.
Amara looks at her then. She has flour on the end of her nose. She doesn't know it.
Elsie reaches up and wipes the flour off Amara's nose with her thumb. She shows her the thumb.
Amara doesn't look at the thumb. She looks at Elsie's mouth, and away, fast, at the oven.
Elsie slides the tins into the cooling oven with the peel, minding it, the way she was told.
While they wait Elsie washes the bowl. She hums again, the low wandering tune from the barrow.
Behind her, at the counter, someone hums the next two notes. Low and warm. Then stops dead.
Elsie doesn't turn round. She keeps washing the bowl, slowly, and hums the next two herself.
A long moment. Behind her Amara hums two more, very quietly. Elsie scrubs the bowl and doesn't look.
They go on like that, two notes each, back and forth, until the cakes smell done.
Elsie takes them out. She turns round at last. Amara has both hands pressed flat over her mouth.
Her eyes are wet and wide. She says, through her hands, that she did that with someone listening.
Elsie says she wasn't listening. She was washing a bowl. Very hard. Amara laughs, wet.
Elsie wraps six warm honey cakes in brown paper for Amara and twists the ends shut.
Amara hugs the parcel, then all at once hugs Elsie, parcel and all, her face in Elsie's hair.
She says, muffled, that she'll look for the boat with the pink head in it. She lets go.
Amara goes out under the lanterns toward the bridge. She looks back twice, and once more.
Up in the attic Elsie winds the new skein into a ball by the round window.
She knits the third finger by candlelight, with the canal lanterns red and gold below.
She knits the fourth finger, the little one, shorter. Her eyes keep closing. She keeps going.
She casts off and breaks the wool. She turns the glove right side out and smooths it flat.
She lays it beside the first on the sill. Two grey gloves, a pair, long-fingered, palm to palm.
She tucks the lavender sprig between them and wraps them in brown paper. She ties it with string.
On the paper she draws a little lantern, so Cora will know, and nothing else.
She opens her notebook to the Midsummer page. Beside the long straight hair she writes: yes!
She looks at the boat a long while. Small, at the very back, she draws the head with braids again.
She looks at it. This time she doesn't rub it out.
She tells Moonpenny about the boat, and the bell, and Noor's yes, and the two notes in the kitchen.
She puts the parcel in her satchel, ready, and buckles it, and sets the satchel by the door.
She blows out the candle and lies down under the sloping roof. She hugs her pillow.
Below on Thimble Canal a late punt goes by under the lit lanterns, its pole knocking on the bridges.
